newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: E.EUROPE MKTS WEATHER U.S. RATE HIKE, FEAR REMAINS.
newsitem.headline: E.EUROPE MKTS WEATHER U.S. RATE HIKE, FEAR REMAINS.

text.p: East European markets on Wednesday weathered the storm of the U.S. Federal Reserve decision to raise interest rates, but analysts warned that a rumoured second increase in May could have severe consequences.
Markets in Prague, Warsaw, Budapest, Bratislava all gained ground, while a drop in Slovenian shares was due more to a sustained downtrend than the move in U.S. rates.
Analysts said that the 25 basis point hike announced on Tuesday by the Fed had already been built into the market, minimising the effect on shares across the region.
"(U.S. Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan did what he did and it (the rate rise) was already priced in," said Bogdan Kornacki, a trader at Wielkopolski Bank Kredytowy (WBK) brokerage.
Added Gyorgy Czipo of ING Barings in Budapest: "There was a factor of uncertainty (before the rate hike), everybody withheld and now they seem to buy heavily."
The hike was the first in over two years in the U.S., and was mainly seen as an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track.

The quarter-percentage-point increase brought the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans up to 5.50 percent. The Fed left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.
But some economists warned that if U.S. economic growth and inflation continue to rise, another rate increase could be in the cards in May.
"With the low presence of foreign investors on the Czech market over the past few weeks, the reaction hasn't been dramatic," said Radek Vavra of Citibank in Prague.
"But...if the Fed raises rates again on May 20, it will be a strong signal to all of the markets here, and cause a strong change in sentiment."

Slovak brokers said the Bratislava bourse also lacks foreign players at the moment, adding that the country's forex market remained calm as well since its interest rate differential is still high enough to retain investor interest.
"Those foreign players who are here mostly play on the interest rate differential, which still remain high enough to bring high profits," said Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB Bank.
The Slovak interbank market on Thursday again rose near to record levels, with shorter-term funds at about 26 perecent and the longer-term deposits at between 17 to 18 percent.
One of the few bourses to lose ground on the day was Ljubljana, but this was attributable almost solely to domestic factors, analysts said.

The Slovenian market has been in a tailspin since the central bank moved in February to block foreign buying by ordering international portfolio investors to open custody accounts at one of Slovenia's 14 fully licensed banks in order to trade in Slovenian securities.
Since the move, the SBI index has fallen 24 percent.
